stem: A 7-year-old girl is reviewed after blunt head trauma and imaging confirms a skull fracture; she is currently stable. Which teaching point best supports ongoing vigilance?

options.text: Skull fractures carry an increased risk of intracranial injury
Skull fractures are usually the most common paediatric chest injury
Skull fractures only matter if there are external signs of thoracic trauma
Skull fractures are mainly concerning because they predict positive FAST findings
Skull fractures are expected to be managed as outpatient burns

explanation: Skull fractures carry an increased risk of intracranial injury. This is because a skull fracture is a marker of potential associated intracranial trauma, so ongoing neurological vigilance is needed even when observations are initially stable.

citations.title: Louisa Leone MD3 2025 - Child and Adolescent Health - Study Notes.pdf

rationale: Skull fracture is a risk marker for intracranial injury, and initial stability does not remove the need for continued neurological concern.

optionExplanations.A: Correct because a skull fracture is associated with a higher risk of intracranial injury and therefore requires ongoing vigilance.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect because this refers to chest trauma, not skull fractures.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect because the significance of a skull fracture is not determined by thoracic signs.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect because FAST is used for abdominal trauma assessment, not for skull fracture risk.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect because burns management is unrelated to skull fracture care.
